newsitem.title: CHINA: Full day for HK's Tung despite handover holiday.
newsitem.headline: Full day for HK's Tung despite handover holiday.

text.p: Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa had a full diplomatic schedule on Wednesday, while the rest of the territory had one more day off to contemplate its return to Chinese rule.

A day after announcing his economic and social agenda, Tung was to have talks with the foreign ministers of Japan, Canada, South Korea, Thailand, New Zealand and the Philippines, attend a parade to celebrate the handover and meet Chinese Vice Premier Qian Qichen.
Most of the rest of Hong Kong was enjoying the last day of a five-day holiday before banks, offices and financial markets reopen on Thursday and the territory returns to its usual frenetic pace.
Celebrations and demonstrations shared the spotlight on Tuesday, Hong Kong's first day as a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China after 156 years as a British colony.
Up to 10,000 activists marched to call on their new leaders to restore democracy after an elected legislature was dissolved with the handover and replaced by a Beijing-picked assembly.

"We want democracy. We want it now," they chanted in the biggest challenge so far to Tung, a shipping magnate who took over as chief executive after the British bowed out at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday.
But Tung declared in a speech: "Democracy is the hallmark of a new era for Hong Kong."

He said Hong Kong must remain "the world's freest and most vibrant economy" as he unveiled a bold policy agenda, pledging action to reduce the astronomical cost of housing, improve educational opportunities at overcrowded schools and take steps to upgrade the territory's technological base.
The South China Morning Post newspaper said in an editorial that Tung "has an inspiring vision for the SAR, but some goals may be elusive."

"But Mr Tung has one advantage that most government heads only dream of," it said. "With a surplus of HK$320 billion (US$41 billion) at his disposal, there is no need to dig deep into the funds to find sufficient money to significantly improve education, housing and care of the elderly."

Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who returned to Beijing after receiving Hong Kong from Britain's Prince Charles, said he wanted China's latest and richest region "forever vigorous and dynamic" with autonomy and freedoms.

Despite such assurances, the arrival of 4,000 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops backed by armoured personnel carriers was to some a provocative reminder of the massacre of demonstrators around Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen pledged that Beijing would never put soldiers on Hong Kong's streets in armoured cars and that elections would be held by May, a date already named by Tung.
While the demonstrators marched through Central district, other people offered a warm welcome to the PLA soldiers.
"I'm definitely happy, I've been waiting for this to happen for years. They are here to liberate us from the British," said Mang Kam, 74, waving a Chinese flag.
Hong Kong also celebrated with 20 tonnes of fireworks, which lit the sky to oohs, ahs and applause from a crowd of several hundred thousand people lining both sides of Victoria Harbour.
